title: Come, Lord Jesus (Apocalypse 22:17–21)
carry: take the water of life, freely

segments.voice: Yesterday, tabernacle: the city coming down, and every tear wiped away. Your line was behold, I make all things new. Who did you comfort? Day six hundred thirty-one.

Back on day three hundred thirty-two, we opened a library, not a book, and started at the first page: in the beginning. Since then, Genesis, the kings, the prophets, the psalms, the Gospels, the letters, the visions. Today we turn the last page. And the Bible doesn't end with a summary, or a moral, or a final warning. It ends with a conversation. Someone says come. Someone answers I'm coming. And then the last prayer in the whole book, three words long. An older form of it turns up in one of Paul's letters, in another language.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF THE LIBRARY.` → `NOT A SUMMARY: A CONVERSATION.` → `THE BIBLE'S LAST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: First, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the spirit and the bride say: Come. And he that heareth, let him say: Come." The Spirit and the bride, the Church, call out to Christ. Then the invitation turns around, toward anyone listening: let him that thirsts come, and take the water of life, freely. Come goes both ways. Then Christ answers: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." That's the Bible's last prayer. Come, Lord Jesus. Now go back to Paul. Writing in Greek to the Corinthians, he leaves one Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha. Aramaic was the language of Jesus and his first followers in Galilee. Paul keeps the word the way you'd keep a word from a grandmother's language, because no other word feels right. It can be read two ways, and scholars discuss which: maran atha, our Lord has come; or marana tha, our Lord, come! Christians can pray both. He has come; come again. An early Christian handbook called the Didache puts maranatha in its prayers after the Eucharist. And come, Lord Jesus, in the Apocalypse, sounds, to some scholars, like that same old prayer, put into Greek. The Bible ends, finally, with a blessing: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." Catholics pray this longing at every Mass. After the Lord's Prayer, the priest prays for the people as they wait in hope for the coming of our Savior. And all through Advent, the Church sings come. The book whose first page has God saying let there be light ends with his people saying come.
screen: `THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY: COME.` · `SURELY I COME QUICKLY.` · `MARANATHA: OUR LORD, COME.` · `PRAYED AT EVERY MASS AND IN ADVENT.` · then, large: `AMEN. COME, LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray come, Lord Jesus, or sit with the longing. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Think of what in your life, or in the world, most needs to be made new: a sorrow, a war, an illness, a relationship. Hold it gently. If you pray, you can say the Bible's last prayer on each out-breath: come, Lord Jesus. Or the old Aramaic word: maranatha, four soft syllables, ma-ra-na-tha. Let it slow down until it's almost a whisper. If you don't pray, just let yourself feel what it's like to long for something to come. The bell holds the time.
Maranatha. Aramaic, from the first Christians: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. The Bible's last prayer. Today's word.

Your line: take the water of life, freely. Today, pause once and drink something slowly, water if you can, and let it remind you of the invitation. And that's the Apocalypse: an unveiling, the first and the last, first charity, not lukewarm, the knock, holy, the Lamb, every tongue, the woman, Babylon, the supper, tabernacle, and maranatha. The last page. Day six hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics voice this longing at every Mass, in the prayer after the Lord's Prayer that speaks of waiting for the coming of the Savior, and especially in Advent, the season of preparing for Christ's coming; some pray maranatha as a short, repeated prayer.

original.note: Aramaic words written in Greek letters (1 Corinthians 16:22): our Lord, come.

trapdoor: what you thought: maranatha is a church name or a worship song.
what it means: an Aramaic prayer of the first Christians, our Lord, come, which the Bible's last prayer echoes: come, Lord Jesus.
what a scholar hears: kept untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22, found in the Didache's Eucharistic prayers (10:6), and rendered in Greek at Apocalypse 22:20.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the claim that the first Christians prayed maranatha before any New Testament page was finished, the Didache date and 'the remarkable part'; the Apocalypse-as-maranatha link is now what some scholars hear.
Maranatha divisions (maran atha / marana tha) and the view that Apocalypse 22:20 renders it in Greek: common scholarly positions. Confirm.
Didache dated 'around the end of the first century'; estimates range from the mid-first to the early second century. Confirm phrasing; Didache 10:6 contains 'Maranatha'.

The prayer after the Lord's Prayer at Mass (the embolism) is described, not quoted (current English text not public domain). The earlier wording 'wait in joyful hope' (1973 ICEL) was replaced with a plain paraphrase, since the current Missal reads differently.
'The first Christians spoke Aramaic' narrowed to the first Christians in Galilee and Jerusalem; Greek-speaking believers were present very early (Acts 6). Confirm.
Carry kept exactly as the index has it: 'come, lord jesus' (lowercase). Consider an owner-approved index change to 'come, Lord Jesus'.
Closes Block H (the Apocalypse, days 619–631) and the reading of the Bible in order begun on day 332; the carry's list uses the index words/lines for days 619–631.
The original-language game shows the Greek-letter transliteration of the Aramaic; confirm, or replace with Aramaic script after review.
